title: Rubio Unveils Cybercrime Visa Crackdown as US Tightens Rules for Students and Journalists
excerpt: Secretary of State announces new visa restrictions targeting cybercriminals and their families, adding to sweeping changes that impose a four-year cap on student visas and 240-day limits for foreign journalists.
body:
• Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a new visa restriction policy targeting individuals complicit in cybercrime, cyber scams, and sextortion — including their immediate family members.
  • The policy follows a DHS rule ending "duration of status" for student and journalist visas, imposing a four-year cap on F-1 and J-1 holders effective September 15.
  • Indian students — over 363,000 enrolled in U.S. universities — face the biggest impact, as PhD programs in science and engineering average 5.6 years to complete.
  • The post-graduation grace period for F-1 visa holders has been halved from 60 days to 30 days, and students can no longer switch programs or institutions.

New Visa Restrictions Target Cybercriminals

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday announced a global visa restriction policy targeting foreign nationals responsible for or complicit in cybercrime and cyber-enabled crime, marking the latest in a rapid-fire series of immigration enforcement actions by the Trump administration.

The policy, implemented under the Immigration and Nationality Act, covers individuals involved in cyberscams and sextortion, and extends to their immediate family members. Rubio singled out Chinese transnational criminal organizations, which he said defrauded American citizens of at least $10 billion in 2024 alone while fueling corruption, money laundering, and human trafficking.

"By restricting visa issuance to those who are responsible for or complicit in these criminal enterprises, we are sending a clear message: The United States will go after those who prey on our citizens."

— Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State

The announcement follows a Trump executive order earlier this year titled "Combatting Cybercrime, Fraud, and Predatory Schemes Against American Citizens," which directed federal agencies to develop measures against foreign scam centers and transnational criminal organizations. Rubio said the administration is deploying sanctions, prosecutions, asset seizures, extradition requests, and international law enforcement cooperation to dismantle criminal networks.

The cybercrime visa policy also comes on the heels of a July 16 visa restriction targeting members of far-left and aligned terrorist groups, according to a State Department statement, reinforcing the administration's broader strategy to block foreign nationals linked with violent and criminal activities from entering the country.

Student Visa Overhaul Hits Indian Community Hardest

The cybercrime restrictions land amid a separate but related upheaval in U.S. immigration policy: the Department of Homeland Security's decision to end the decades-old "duration of status" system for international students, exchange visitors, and foreign journalists.

Under the new DHS rule, published in the Federal Register and set to take effect September 15, holders of F-1 student visas and J-1 exchange visas will be admitted for the length of their approved program — but capped at a maximum of four years. Foreign journalists on I visas face a 240-day limit, shortened to just 90 days for Chinese journalists.

The changes will affect roughly 1.2 million international students and about 1,500 foreign journalists currently in the United States, according to the Migration Policy Institute and the U.S. State Department. Students already in the country under the old system will automatically transition to the new framework, with their stay capped at four years from the rule's effective date.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the move. "For nearly half a century, the outdated 'duration of status' system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud," he said in a statement.

PhD Students Face an Impossible Timeline

The four-year cap poses a particular challenge for doctoral candidates. On average, it takes 5.6 years for students in the United States to complete a PhD in science or engineering, according to data cited by Nature. Students who exceed the limit must apply to USCIS for an extension, undergoing biometric verification, background checks, and fraud screening — a process with no guaranteed outcome.

The rule also prohibits graduate students on F-1 visas from switching programs or institutions, and slashes the post-graduation grace period from 60 days to 30 days. There were approximately 488,000 international graduate students in the United States during the 2024–25 academic year.

"For decades, international students have been encouraged to come and study in the United States. These restrictions mark the dissolution of the dream of becoming a leading US innovator and scientist."

— Bennett Goldberg, Physicist, Northwestern University

Press freedom advocates have also raised concerns. Gabe Rottman, vice president of policy at the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, warned that the new journalist visa limits risk giving the government leverage to deny renewals in retaliation for critical coverage.

What This Means for the Indian Diaspora

Indian students represent the single largest international student community in the United States. According to the Open Doors 2025 report, 363,019 Indian students were enrolled at U.S. colleges and universities during the 2024–25 academic year — accounting for nearly 31% of all international students.

Many pursue master's and doctoral programs in STEM fields that routinely extend beyond four years, making the new cap a direct threat to academic plans already in motion. The tighter restrictions on program transfers and the shortened grace period compound the uncertainty, particularly for students who may need to transition to H-1B or other work visas after graduation.

India has previously intervened diplomatically on student visa issues. In mid-2025, New Delhi pressed Washington to evaluate Indian student visa applications "on merit" after the administration instituted a temporary suspension of visa interviews and intensified social media background checks for applicants, according to The Indian Eye.

What Comes Next

The cybercrime visa restrictions take effect immediately. The student and journalist visa overhaul is scheduled for September 15, giving universities and students roughly two months to prepare. Universities are already reviewing compliance requirements, and educational institutions have begun advising current and prospective students to factor the new timeline into their academic planning.

Together, the two policy actions represent the most significant tightening of U.S. visa rules in decades — one aimed at criminal networks, the other reshaping the legal framework for millions of legitimate visitors. For the Indian diaspora, the combined effect adds a layer of bureaucratic risk to an already complex immigration landscape.
